title: Round or right-sized?
hook: Put two identical circles on a world map. Can the map keep both honest?

knows: that Mercator makes high latitudes look big
doesNotKnow: what an equal-area map costs in return
that no flat map can keep both shape and area

misconception: An accurate map would simply show everything at the right size and shape.
objective: The learner can explain that Mercator keeps small circles round but swells them about four times at 60°N, that Equal Earth keeps their areas but squashes them, and that no flat map can do both.

claims.text: On this Mercator map a 1,000 km circle at 60°N is drawn about 4.2 times the area of the same circle on the equator.
claims.source: Ratio of d3 geoPath areas of geoCircle (radius 8.99 degrees = 1,000 km on R = 6,371.0088 km, precision 0.5 degrees) at (70 E, 60 N) and (8 E, 0) on the lesson's own Mercator projection: 4.158 (artifacts/scratch/w1-tissot.mjs). The readout and reveal compute the same quantity live, so they cannot disagree.

claims.text: Mercator stretches 2 times east-west and 2 times north-south at 60°, so areas there are 4 times larger; a 1,000 km circle comes out a bit more because its top reaches 69°N.
claims.source: Snyder (1987), Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395, ch. 7: h = k = sec(latitude), area factor sec^2; sec^2 60 = 4. Circle top latitude 60 + 8.99 = 68.99 N.

claims.text: Mercator keeps small circles round (it is conformal).
claims.source: Snyder (1987) ch. 7. At 1,000 km radius the drawn circle is very slightly egg-shaped (wider at the top); the lesson says 'still round'.

claims.text: On Equal Earth the two circles' areas match, but the northern one is squashed.
claims.source: Equal Earth is equal-area (Savric, Patterson and Jenny 2018, IJGIS 33(3): 454-465); the lesson's own path-area ratio is 1.000 at 0, 30, 45 and 60 N (w1-tissot.mjs). Squashing: the 60 N circle's drawn bounding box is 74 x 43 px against 48 x 65 px for the equator circle. No number for the shape change is shown.

claims.text: No flat map can keep shapes and areas both true everywhere; this is a theorem about spheres.
claims.source: Conformal (h = k) plus equal-area (h k = 1) would force h = k = 1, an isometry, which Gauss's Theorema Egregium (1827) rules out for a sphere (Gaussian curvature 1/R^2, not 0). Snyder (1987) ch. 1.

claims.text: Both circles have a 1,000 km radius on the globe.
claims.source: geoCircle radius 1,000 / 6,371.0088 rad = 8.993 degrees; spherical cap area 3.14 million km2 for both (geoArea).

recall.question: A map keeps every country's area exactly right. What must it give up?
options: Nothing: it can keep shapes right too
Shapes: some countries will look squashed or stretched
recall.why: A sphere cannot be flattened without distortion; an equal-area map must distort shapes, and a shape-keeping (conformal) map must distort areas.
